title: Venus walks into a restaurant
sceneAlt: BoJack stands in Elefante beneath a large parody of Botticelli's Birth of Venus, with an elephant in the shell.
artAlt: Sandro Botticelli's The Birth of Venus, showing Venus standing on a shell as figures blow wind toward her.
lede: Elefante turns Botticelli’s Venus into a sight gag: keep the shell, swap in an elephant.
story: BoJack buys a restaurant and calls it Elefante. On the wall, Botticelli’s Venus has become an elephant standing in the same shell, surrounded by the same wind and drapery. DailyArt identifies the restaurant appearance in S1E07, while Hyperallergic traces the image to the first season. The gag works without an art-history lesson. A famous entrance has been rebuilt for Hollywoo, where every arrival is also a performance. The mural sits behind BoJack as he raises a glass, placing his own performance in front of it. Botticelli presents Venus to the shore and to the viewer. Elefante presents its subject to a dining room full of people who are busy presenting themselves. That connection is my reading. The scene and painting are documented in the sources below.
reading: The shell survives the parody because the entrance is the joke.

episode: Opening episodes · BoJack's office / S1E11 · hallucination
title: Two figures, one pool
artwork: Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)
sceneAlt: BoJack and Diane stand in his office beneath the pool painting that recurs throughout the series.
artAlt: David Hockney's Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures), with one figure swimming toward another who stands at the edge.
lede: A swimmer crosses the blue water. A clothed figure stands at the edge. The distance between them fills the frame.
story: A version of David Hockney’s pool painting hangs in BoJack’s office while he performs the role of a successful actor. Hyperallergic identifies it in the opening episode, and DailyArt labels the circulated office frame S1E02. The composition returns in the S1E11 hallucination, so the pool becomes part of the show’s memory rather than a one-scene reference. Hockney made the original after a breakup. Its two figures share a frame but little else: one swims away while the other remains dressed and still. In the office, BoJack and Diane stand beneath the same division. That distance fits BoJack’s relationships with uncomfortable precision. The show offers no published creator statement that fixes this meaning. The connection comes from the painting’s placement, its return, and the scenes that gather around it.
reading: The figures share a picture, not a world.

episode: S5E02 · The Dog Days Are Over
title: The bridge falls
sceneAlt: Diane sits in her bare new apartment, where a Monet-inspired print hangs on the wall.
artAlt: Claude Monet's The Japanese Footbridge, a green bridge crossing a dense water garden.
lede: Diane hangs a garden scene in her bare apartment. Then she closes the door and the print drops from the wall.
story: In S5E02, Diane leaves her life with Mr. Peanutbutter and moves into a cheap apartment. The print on the wall resembles Monet’s Japanese Footbridge and his water-lily paintings, as DailyArt and Sartle note. It is the room’s one view of somewhere lush, tended, and complete. The rest of the apartment is sparse and temporary. Diane closes the door. The print falls. The joke is physical and blunt: even the borrowed landscape will not stay put. Monet’s bridge does not stand for divorce, and the show gives us no reason to treat it as a code. Its placement does sharpen the scene. Diane wants a clean passage into a new life, but she has moved into a room where the fixtures barely hold.
reading: She wants a clean crossing. The wall cannot hold the picture.

title: Ophelia above the bed
sceneAlt: A scene from Sarah Lynn's bedroom where Millais's Ophelia hangs above the bed.
artAlt: John Everett Millais's Ophelia, showing a woman floating in a river surrounded by flowers.
lede: Millais painted Ophelia floating toward death. Sarah Lynn sleeps beneath her.
story: Sarah Lynn’s bedroom holds the bright, expensive debris of a child star’s life. Above the bed hangs a version of Millais’s Ophelia, the Pre-Raphaelite painting of Shakespeare’s character floating in a river. DailyArt identifies the reference in S3E11. Its position matters: the painting sits above Sarah Lynn before the episode reaches its final act. Flowers surround Ophelia while her open hands drift at the surface. Nothing about the reference explains Sarah Lynn, and the creators have not published a statement that assigns it a single meaning. Still, the pairing is hard to dismiss. The room turns a woman’s death into beautiful décor while Sarah Lynn’s danger remains in plain sight. After the episode ends, the flowers and dark water are difficult to see as background detail.
reading: The warning is visible. Everyone has learned to live with it.

episode: S6E01 · A Horse Walks into a Rehab
title: A self-portrait in rehab
sceneAlt: BoJack sits in his Pastiches rehab room beneath a van Gogh-inspired self-portrait of a goat.
artAlt: Vincent van Gogh's 1889 Self-Portrait, a green-coated figure against a restless blue background.
lede: BoJack checks into Pastiches and finds Van Gogh recast as a goat on the bedroom wall.
story: In S6E01, a goat version of Van Gogh’s 1889 self-portrait hangs in BoJack’s room at Pastiches. DailyArt and Sartle identify the reference. The animal substitution lands as a quick joke, but the setting gives it weight. Van Gogh painted the original during a period of illness and recovery. BoJack arrives at rehab with a long record of harm and a habit of treating that harm as personality. The show later uses another Van Gogh self-portrait in a different facility, which turns the first reference into a pattern. This parallel is not a diagnosis, and no published creator statement claims that it is. The portrait gives the scene a harder question: BoJack can describe himself in painful detail, but can he change what he sees?
reading: Self-knowledge names the damage. It does not repair it.
